name: Zélie Pichon
languages: Louisiana Creole French (from her father, who will speak nothing else at the supper table)
equipment: Car: 1940 Ford Deluxe sedan, black, "Duchess", painted with the Tremé Taxi Company's number 14 on the doors and a dome light she can switch off
Snub-nose .38 (Smith & Wesson Chiefs-pattern, bought from a sailor), 5 rounds loaded, in a clip under the dash
Tire iron, under the front seat where a policeman will not think it a weapon
City street guide, annotated in her own hand with which streets flood
Driving gloves, kid, a present from her father
Her hack licence, which reads COLORED, and a city ordinance she can quote about whom a colored cab may carry
A notebook of fares: who went where, when, with whom
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin, New Orleans: she always knows the quickest way across a neighbourhood on foot or by car, which alleys go through, and which bars and garages belong to whom; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city; once per foot chase the GM introduces the next complication for her pursuer instead of her)

Behind the Wheel (Wheelman: advantage on Driving checks in chases and to avoid crashing; in Duchess, +15 to the car's hit points (5 x level) and her proficiency bonus to its AC while she drives; once per long rest when Duchess would drop to 0 hit points, she drops to 1 and keeps running; she can repair Duchess on a short rest)
Smooth Ride (Wheelman: her passengers do not have disadvantage on ranged attacks from the moving car, and have advantage on saves in a crash or ram)
Lead Foot (Wheelman, 2nd level: on each turn, a bonus action to Dash, Disengage or Hide on foot, or one extra maneuver while driving)
Style: Getaway Man (Wheelman, 3rd level: as the quarry in a chase she escapes with a lead of 2 rounds instead of 3, and she always knows two ways out of any neighbourhood)

Nobody Looks at the Cabbie (Cab Driver background: she can wait outside a building for hours without anyone thinking about her, and passengers say things in the back seat they would not say to a priest)

personality.traits: I drive fast, talk fast and laugh at my own jokes before the end. I know every pothole between the river and the lake by name. I am never, ever late, and I never let a white man see that I am frightened of him, which is not the same as not being frightened.
personality.ideals: Nobody owns me and nobody owns Duchess. I paid for her myself, every cent, and I will be my own boss in this city if it kills me, which it may.
personality.bonds: My father, Anatole Pichon, master plasterer, the finest hands in the Seventh Ward, who has made the faces on Carnival floats for thirty years for men who would not shake his hand. The Tremé Taxi Company and the other drivers, who look after each other because no one else will.
personality.flaws: I take risks for the pleasure of it. I am proud enough to refuse help I need, and I hold a grudge like a jar holds pickles.

appearance: A small, quick woman of twenty-seven with a round face, freckles across a light brown nose, a gap between her front teeth she shows when she grins, and hair pinned up under a man's tweed cap. Brown horsehide jacket with the elbows gone pale, driving gloves, sensible shoes and a man's wristwatch.
backstory: Zélie Pichon was born on Annette Street in the Seventh Ward, the only daughter of Anatole Pichon, the plasterer, and grew up in his shop among buckets of plaster of Paris, horsehair, gold leaf and the enormous pale faces of Carnival gods and sea monsters that he sculpted every winter for the white krewes' floats. She learned to drive on her uncle's ice truck at twelve. When the men went to war in 1942, the Tremé Taxi Company, one of the city's Black-owned cab companies, which by city ordinance may carry only Black passengers, hired its first woman driver, and she has never stopped. She bought Duchess outright in 1944 with three years of savings and named her for the way she rides. She knows the city from the back of the cab: who goes to which address at two in the morning, which policemen stop colored cabs for sport, and which streets on the Ninth Ward side of the Industrial Canal flood in a hard rain. On Thursday night, 28 February, at a quarter past nine, she was waiting for a fare at the St. Claude Avenue bridge and saw a long grey car come fast off Jourdan Avenue from the direction of the Ste. Claire yard with its lights off. She did not think about it until she heard about the body.
